rewrites.summary:
Kogi stands under Nigeria's uniform criminalisation framework: the national same-sex marriage prohibition law carries up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex conduct and also reaches people who help arrange or attend same-sex weddings. An allied government's August 2026 travel advice warns LGBT+ travellers across Nigeria of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation. The constitution offers no specific protections for sexual orientation, and no federal anti-discrimination protections exist.

Trans-specific risk is documented nationally and applies in full here: mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people are reported as common, especially in northern states, and the 2024 beating-death of a prominent transgender creator in the capital — after an earlier stabbing she had said left her fearing for her life — evidences lethal violence against visibly trans people, with an investigation announced but no accountability recorded in the sources. The national penalties apply in full in this state; no local divergence is claimed in either direction.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Litigation flux in the parent nation: in 2022 a coalition of human rights organisations won a court ruling that three sections of the 2013 same-sex marriage prohibition act breached the constitution and could not be enforced anywhere in the country, effectively allowing LGBTQ+ organisations and individuals to exist and organise; the sources record no similar ruling for the conduct and marriage-prohibition provisions.

Neighbour comparison: a framework source lists twelve northern states/provinces applying Sharia (religious) criminal law with harsher penalties, including death penalties in two states/provinces for lesbianism, and the travel advice reports some northern states/provinces can prescribe the death penalty; the sources do not identify this state/province among the Sharia-administering group.
rewrites.localsOnly: No resident-specific sources survived audit for this state: the dossier records no local cultural-role, birth-register or resident-discrimination data specific to the state, and the mass-arrest reporting and the 2024 killing are national-level evidence rather than state-specific documentation.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: No state-specific source survived audit for this state, so no local divergence is claimed in either direction; the sources do not identify the state among the northern states/provinces applying Sharia (religious) criminal provisions, and the 2022 ruling leaves the conduct and marriage-prohibition provisions standing. No source in the dossier addresses border-screening, documents or passport-marker practice for trans visitors to this state. The killing investigation was announced but no accountability is recorded in the sources.

National-framework reference entry that applies in full here: the same-sex marriage (prohibition) act 2013, passed by the elected national legislature on 30 May 2013 and signed into law in January 2014, makes entering a same-sex marriage or civil union liable to 14 years' imprisonment and makes registering, operating or participating in 'gay clubs, societies and organisations' or making a public show of a same-sex amorous relationship liable to 10 years' imprisonment. The criminal code separately criminalises sex between men with up to 14 years' imprisonment and gross indecency with up to 3 years, while twelve states/provinces applying religious criminal law impose harsher penalties, with death penalties applied in two states/provinces for lesbianism. In 2022 a court ruled that three sections of the 2013 act breached the constitution and could not be enforced anywhere in the country, effectively allowing LGBTQ+ organisations and individuals to exist and organise; the entry records no similar ruling for the conduct and marriage-prohibition provisions. It also notes the constitution has no specific protections for sexual orientation and that there are no national anti-discrimination protections.

An allied government's August 2026 travel advice warns LGBT+ travellers across Nigeria of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation.

Trans-specific risk is documented nationally: mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people are reported as common, especially in northern states, with tens of arrests per year and police and religious-police harassment including beatings, blackmail, extortion and torture recorded in the country-policy note; the 2024 beating-death of a prominent transgender creator in the capital — after an earlier stabbing she had said left her fearing for her life — evidences lethal violence against visibly trans people, with no accountability recorded. Neighbour comparison: the country-policy note reports religious penal codes applying to Muslims in the twelve northern states/provinces with death as the maximum penalty for men, and at least four religious death sentences imposed since 2022 with none carried out; the framework source names the twelve states/provinces and this state/province is not among them, so the religious tier does not reach it.

rewrites.summary:
Ekiti stands under Nigeria's uniform criminalisation framework: the same-sex marriage prohibition law carries up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex conduct and also reaches people who help arrange or attend same-sex weddings.
